title: ‘Joker’ Composer Hildur Gudnadottir Confirms She’s Scoring Sarah Polley’s ‘The Bell Jar,’ Starring Billie Eilish
description:
Composer Hildur Guðnadóttir, who won an Oscar with “Joker,” is already deep into “The Bell Jar.”

	Sarah Polley’s Sylvia Plath adaptation, which rec
body:
Composer Hildur Guðnadóttir, who won an Oscar with “Joker,” is already deep into “The Bell Jar.”

	Sarah Polley’s Sylvia Plath adaptation, which recently wrapped, will give pop icon Billie Eilish her first starring role, while offering the composer a new kind of creative partnership.

	“[Working with a fellow Oscar-winning musician like Eilish] makes a huge difference,” Guðnadóttir tells Variety. “You know she understands the process that goes into writing music, so what you write can really resonate with her.”
	

	Building on a relationship forged on 2022’s Oscar-winning “Women Talking,” Guðnadóttir joined Polley’s latest project early, writing themes the filmmaker could play on set. She was equally keen to connect with Eilish before the singer stepped in front of the camera.


	“We talked about what we envisioned for the music, and how we could translate what Sylvia experiences into it,” Guðnadóttir says. “For me, the core of Plath’s writing is that she’s searching for identity. She keeps asking, ‘Who am I?’ and then uses her writing to understand that. Billie, Sarah and I have been exploring how we hear that, how to translate it into music, and what music Sylvia herself might have been listening to.”

	Guðnadóttir calls the film a career highlight. 

	“It’s one of the most exciting projects I’ve ever done,” she says. “Sarah and I are good friends, so getting to tell this story with her is amazing. I think it’s one of the most amazing books ever written.”

	“You can feel it in every word Sylvia Plath writes,” she continues. “This burning need and yearning to find herself through her writing. I’ve been reading a lot of her work, including her books, essays and poems, and it’s vast. People tend to remember the drama of her story, that she had mental health struggles and a sad end. But her writing is so full of life, creativity and energy, and that’s what people tend to forget. I really hope this film can bring that back to center and celebrate her magnificent way of living.”
	

	Variety caught up with the composer at this year’s World Soundtrack Awards in Ghent, where she was guest of honor. Hours before her trip to Belgium, Guðnadóttir was still mixing “Enemies,” the Ari Aster-produced A24 thriller. Directed by Henry Dunham and starring Jeremy Allen White and Austin Butler, the Chicago-shot cop drama let her play with urban ambient sounds. 

	“I find it really interesting how the sounds of the city work with the film,” she says. “I’m working a lot with environmental textures and city sounds, and how they can relate to the film’s music. Listening is always at the heart, along with my curiosity.”

	Guðnadóttir would also love to return to the “28 Years Later” franchise, whenever the next installment arrives. At the World Soundtrack Awards, she described the “nerve-wracking” experience of watching the first in the new series, scored by Young Fathers, after finishing her work on Nia DaCosta’s “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.”

	“I never got to hear a single note or see a single frame of [Danny Boyle’s ‘28 Years Later’] while I was working [on ‘The Bone Temple’],” she says. 

	“I kept asking whether we should have some connective tissue between the scores, but it was a deliberate decision to keep the two completely separate. So when part one came out, I went to the cinema with everyone else. I was sitting there thinking, ‘Please work together, please work together,’ because I had already delivered my part and couldn’t change a thing. It was funny, but nerve-wracking!” 

	The description could apply to the series as a whole.

	“The amazing thing about these stories, and about [‘The Bone Temple’] in particular, is that they look very gory, aggressive and violent, but at the same time, they’re very human, soft and funny,” she says. “I think part two is hilarious. So the question was how could the music amplify that.” 

	DaCosta wanted strings, while Guðnadóttir sought to counter their ethereal quality with something more grounded. Taking the film’s title literally, she turned to an unlikely source for percussion. 

	“I have a friend who runs a hamburger place just outside of Berlin,” she explains. “She has a good relationship with her butcher, so I got a deal to take the leftover bones. All the percussion in the film is made from bones. The shoulder bones made interesting clapping percussion, and the bigger ones suited deeper beating percussion. The smaller ones were better suited to flutes.” 
	

	Bur first, she had to prepare her instruments. 

	“I do everything myself, and that includes boiling the bones,” Guðnadóttir says with a smile. “I’m very hands-on.”

title: ‘Baywatch’ Trailer: Reboot Has Hot People, Big Stunts and Lots of Slow-Motion Running on the Beach
description:
There’s sex, sand and swimsuits in the trailer for Fox’s “Baywatch” reboot, which premieres on the network in January.

	The three-minute clip opens
body:
There’s sex, sand and swimsuits in the trailer for Fox’s “Baywatch” reboot, which premieres on the network in January.

	The three-minute clip opens with series star Stephen Amell leading a rescue mission after a plane collides with a parasail. Amell plays a grown-up version of Hobie Buchannon, the wild child from the original 1990s series. The series follows Hobie, now a Baywatch Captain, following in the footsteps of his father, Mitch, while his world is turned upside down by the surprise arrival of Charlie (Jessica Belkin), the daughter he never knew. Eager to carry on the family legacy, Charlie strives to become a Baywatch lifeguard alongside her dad.
	

	The “Baywatch” reboot was picked up for the 2026-2027 broadcast season by Fox back in September 2025 with a 12-episode order. The series held an open casting call in early 2026 and began production in Los Angeles in the spring.


	Shay Mitchell, Brooks Nader, Hassie Harrison, Livvy Dunne, Noah Beck, David Chokachi and Thaddeus LaGrone star alongside Amell and Belkin. Ashley Moore, Luke Eisner, Nadia Gray, Kylar Miranda, and Charlie McElveen appear in recurring cast roles. Hip-hop superstar Megan Thee Stallion also makes an appearance, as evidenced by the trailer.

	The original “Baywatch” series debuted in 1989 and, at its peak, was the most-watched show in the world, airing in over 200 countries. The ensemble cast included David Hasselhoff as head lifeguard Mitch Buchannon and helped launch the acting careers of stars like Pamela Anderson, Jason Momoa, Yasmine Bleeth and Carmen Electra. The show also spawned the spinoff “Baywatch Nights” and, in 2017, was rebooted as a failed feature film starring Dwayne Johnson and Zac Efron.
	

	Showrunner Matt Nix is an executive producer on the reboot along with McG, Michael Berk, Greg Bonann, Doug Schwartz, Dante Di Loreto and Mike Horowitz. McG also directed the premiere episode. The series is co-produced by Fox Entertainment and Fremantle.

title: Open to AI: Hollywood Is Embracing Artificial Intelligence Tools Despite Doomsday Fears
description: Manhattan Beach Studios in Southern California is a pinnacle of revolutionary technology, home to both the “volume” screens where Jon Favreau filmed
body:
Manhattan Beach Studios in Southern California is a pinnacle of revolutionary technology, home to both the “volume” screens where Jon Favreau filmed the “Mandalorian” franchise and Lightstorm Entertainment, where James Cameron has spent years bringing the Na’vi to life.

	Tucked away at Stage 21 lies Innovative Dreams, an AI offshoot of director Jon Erwin’s Entertainment company Wonder Project. Here, chief operating officer Bryan Yee sips from a Diet Coke can as he showcases the soundstage housing Innovative Dreams’ crown jewel: a collection of LED screens where a team of AI artists weaves generative AI into productions. It’s not the first time the space has been shown to a journalist. But that it’s happened multiple times this year shows that three-quarters of the way into 2026, AI is no longer Hollywood’s ultimate bad word.
	

	The term “AI” has emerged as an addendum to the Hays Code, the 20th-century guidelines dictating what studios should and shouldn’t include in their films. It’s spooked the worlds of corporate and art alike, especially after months of headlines over the potentially world-ending nature of AI models and warnings that progress needs to be paced. Americans are also increasingly believing the tech is doing more harm than good, according to a recent Gallup poll.


	But much like the way studios and directors of the 1960s and ’70s embraced the once-taboo profanity and nudity, this year AI has found a new wave of advocates eager to go public. The technology turned up at marquee film festivals, including Tribeca, which premiered the AI-generated docudrama “Dreams of Violets.” Oscar winner Reese Witherspoon declared that “the AI revolution has begun,” and Martin Scorsese said filmmakers had to be “open to how [film] can evolve.” George Lucas was perhaps the most blunt in a July interview: “There’s nothing you can do about it.”
	

	Part of what’s spurred this breakthrough involves creatives getting to know the technology. Some have found it additive to their projects: Veteran producer Ryan Kavanaugh says his firm, Acme Studios, lowered the cost of Doug Liman’s film “Bitcoin” from $200 million to $70 million with the use of AI. Below-the-line costs on “Bitcoin” were brought down from $130 million to $35 million. Others have experimented with AI features or used AI tools to help with things like audio syncing. Kathleen Kennedy, who served as the president of Lucasfilm from 2012 to 2026, helped organize a group of industry dignitaries to put together a framework for how Hollywood should talk about it.



	

					From the AI-generated docudrama “Dreams of Violets”
									Courtesy of Dreams of Violets
	



	“When you have a set of tools that all of a sudden, ‘I can dream it, and I can create it, and I can show it to somebody,’ what you realize is that it heightens your creativity and did not diminish it at all,” Erwin says.

	But even with such attitudinal strides, Pew Research shows that people’s fears about AI’s societal impact are high, and digital choirs hurl insults at any project featuring the tech. It’s led creatives to walk a tricky line between the wish to experiment with AI and the havoc disclosing its use can wreak.

	“If the creative is great and it engages the audience on a different level than just ‘Hey, look at this thing that’s AI,’ the audience is going to understand it,” says Kathleen Grace, Lionsgate’s chief AI officer. “But it’s challenging when you lead with AI as the only hook.”

	Some directors have gone all in. Oscar-winning director Steven Soderbergh sparked discourse earlier this year when he revealed how he used roughly 10 minutes of AI in his upcoming documentary “John Lennon: The Lost Interview.” He also disclosed his plans to use AI in his Wagner Moura-starring film about the Spanish-American War.

	While Soderbergh recognizes AI remains a “very emotional subject,” he says the loudest voices raging against its use are those that haven’t bothered to engage with it at all. “I’ve seen the version of the John Lennon doc without that material, and I’ve seen the version with the material that we generated, and the version with that material is a better version of the movie,” Soderbergh says. “Here’s what’s really funny to me: If I told people that nine minutes and 40 seconds was VFX that took two and a half million dollars in two years, there would have been no debate at all. So what are we talking about?”
	

	It’s a mindset that “Bourne Identity” director Liman brought to “Bitcoin,” an upcoming Casey Affleck and Gal Gadot-led picture tracing a man’s quest to prove he invented the controversial currency. The project recruited Acme, which specializes in “gray box” soundstages that host real humans while a team of 150 AI artists generates the location imagery and lighting.

	Liman, according to Jed Weintrob, the CEO of Liman’s content studio 30 Ninjas, “likes to push the envelope” and thinks AI tools can be “real superchargers for storytellers.” “We’re creating a world that would be almost financially impossible to make without this technology,” he says.

	Kavanaugh claims the industry shift toward embracing AI was caused by Liman’s decision to go public with his use of it. After the initial disclosure, Acme took several meetings with a mix of studios and filmmakers eager to understand how a project managed to dramatically lower costs. (Kavanaugh wouldn’t disclose the names of the group.)

	After those meetings, Kavanaugh says, the creatives realized that “we’re not killing the art; we’re enhancing the art.“ He adds, “It’s making it more efficient. It’s creating better tool sets. And all of a sudden, we really saw a big shift … from people that we thought were going to be like, ‘No, we can’t do that,’ to ‘Well, can we use it in this show?’”

	Still, such curiosity doesn’t mean all-encompassing acceptance — either by the industry or the audiences that sustain it. This summer alone saw the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences disqualify synthetic performers and AI-written scripts from awards consideration, while the Cannes Film Festival issued a blanket ban on AI-generated productions. When the Urbanworld Film Festival said in June it would accept AI-generated productions for its 30th edition, the Writers Guild of America ended its long-standing sponsorship. The move was consistent with the union’s concerns about the improper use of AI, but it was a choice Urbanworld CEO Stacy Spikes says risks creating a “very slippery slope” — after all, should anyone dictate what tools aspiring filmmakers can experiment with?

	Actors have taken action against the harmful effects of AI. Soderbergh endorsed the Human Consent Foundation, a nonprofit cofounded by Cate Blanchett in June, that created a database where people are encouraged to register how their likenesses can or can’t be pulled by AI models. Blanchett told Variety at the time that while the registry may not revolutionize how people engage with AI, “the more people adopt it, the more chance it has of making a real impact.” She added, “We do have to start somewhere, because thoughtlessness is the enemy of creativity.”
	

	Audiences have also revolted against AI’s intersection with Hollywood, criticizing the initially undisclosed use of the technology for a sequence in Eli Roth’s horror film “Ice Cream Man” and a marketing campaign featuring podcasting dogs for Warner Bros. Discovery’s “The End of Oak Street.”

	Jeffrey Katzenberg, the veteran Hollywood executive who wrote a 2,377-word essay on X last month urging the film industry to work with Silicon Valley and responsibly adopt the technology, says he’s noticed a pervasive sense of “concern and fear” surrounding AI’s presence in Hollywood. The resistance mimics what he calls a pattern of averting “innovation and change.” But, he warns, “to resist technology is to risk irrelevance.”

	Katzenberg is entering the fray himself, developing an AI animation studio that will serve as a vehicle for tools he thinks the industry can adopt. But he hopes to also create a project that could spur a true sentiment shift in the way “Toy Story,” created by his former studio Pixar, did for CGI in the ’90s. “We’ll all know when we see it,” Katzenberg says. “Tools are never the point. What matters is taste, creativity and imagination.”

	For Hollywood to progress, Katzenberg says, it has to accept the wave of change — and progress — AI can bring. It’s part of the ethos of his AI animation studio, capitalizing on what he sees as “a true renaissance for Hollywood storytelling” and “a complete transformation of all forms of video creation.”

	Walking the tightrope between acceptance and resistance puts studios, eager to save money with AI, in a bind. How do you greenlight original stories that may use AI when faced with audiences and creatives wary of the technology? “I don’t really know,” one AI-adopting studio executive admits.

	But a lot of people’s consternation, the executive says, comes from how U.S. political leaders and tech executives are handling the messaging surrounding AI and fears around its impact on jobs, a factor those in Hollywood have little control over. “Right now, the political context of it would be “Well, gee, if you used AI, you displace people’s jobs. You would have hired 1,000 people rather than 100,’” the executive says. “Yeah, that’s probably true.” But, he claims, studios can now make 10 times as many projects due to the efficiency of AI. And more projects will ultimately amount to the same number of people working. No one can argue with the fact that the industry will benefit from having more stories to tell.
	

	Hollywood’s next battle? Getting the AI-powered work produced by industry professionals to resonate with audiences, as opposed to the online video slop made by people without industry experience.

	“The reality is the excellence that you see in cinematic storytelling is because there are creators, directors, filmmakers, costume designers, production designers,” the executive says. “They think very deeply [about] what that experience is going to be. The people creating the slop have not thought deeply about it.”

schema.headline: Open to AI: Hollywood Is Embracing Artificial Intelligence Tools Despite Doomsday Fears

title: How ‘American Girl’ Author Aged Up Samantha Parkington for Adult Historical Fiction Novel: ‘It Would Never Be Spicy’
description:
Mattel’s American Girl brand makes history this week with the release of “Samantha: The Next Chapter,” its first novel for adults.

	Since her intro
body:
Mattel’s American Girl brand makes history this week with the release of “Samantha: The Next Chapter,” its first novel for adults.

	Since her introduction in 1986, Samantha has been widely regarded as one of the most beloved American Girl dolls among the target millennial demographic and picking the Edwardian-era character as the first one used for this adult-historical-fiction-book experiment is a perfect nostalgia play. 


	Written by New York Times bestselling author Fiona Davis, the book catches up with iconic American Girl character Samantha Parkington now at the age of 25 in the year 1920. 
	

	“It was so much fun, I have to say, because the original stories are so full of fun things to play with. And so as I read them, ideas were coming to mind right and left,” Davis tells Variety. “And it made sense she would want to be a teacher because that is her interest as a young girl and also progressive education was going on then. So there was a really wonderful opportunity to bring the history into it a little bit more and show how in 1920, things were really at the cusp of huge change, which is why it was a perfect year to choose.”

	Per the synopsis for “Samantha: The Next Chapter,” “It’s 1920 and 25-year-old Samantha Parkington is working hard to educate women in New York about suffrage and encourage them to vote in their first presidential election that fall. But when Samantha’s large inheritance, including her childhood Mount Bedford home, is stolen in a shocking scheme, she goes from socialite to shop girl overnight and experiences a very different side of New York City. Searching for clues regarding the theft of her inheritance, she infiltrates the business of a notorious criminal in New York City. Determined as ever, Samantha will do whatever it takes to find answers and save her family’s legacy.”
	

	“It was really taking little bits and pieces from those original stories, which were so beautifully detailed and then bringing them to life,” Davis says. “And I think the important thing for me about Samantha was that she’s kind of a paradox where she’s surrounded by wealth. So if you look at her and you think, that girl has everything and then you dig deeper and oh, she’s an orphan. So there’s a hole somewhere in her, and that needs to be filled in a way. And I think that makes her complicated and a really interesting character to pursue as an adult.”

	Read on for more from Variety’s interview with Davis, including spoilers from Samantha’s new book.
	
		How much creative freedom did you have when crafting the “Samantha: The Next Chapter” storyline and how much was suggested by the American Girl brand?	

	In terms of the plot, they gave me so much freedom. I could really do whatever I wanted, and then it was approved by a committee and that kind of thing. But it was really pretty up to me to decide what to do. And at the end, I wanted it to be open-ended so that we could possibly venture into a new phase of her life and they agreed. I think that just keeps the door open.
	
		We see Grandmary, Uncle Gard, Aunt Cornelia and Agatha in this book, but other characters from the Samantha world are only mentioned, like Nellie and live elsewhere. What was the choice behind who to include in the story and who to make reference to?	

	Part of it was that there are certain characters that possibly, maybe there’ll be books about them down the road. So we didn’t want to use up too much, and I’m allowed to say that. So it was a matter of her base family, her extended family, who are very supportive … And [the American Girl brand] encouraged me to really open it up to new faces and new characters in order to launch her as an adult and show that this is a different time and a different age. But then, on top of that, for me, with every character, I want to start off from a place of great vulnerability and have them grow in some way. And so, Samantha’s surrounded by wealth and this extended family that adores her. And my thought, as an author, was, what if all that went away? What if she really has to figure it out on her own using the tenacity that she’s so well known for and her intelligence and her empathy and just set her free in New York to try and figure out what’s going on and solve a mystery and possibly fall in love and grow as a person and see that she is capable of pretty much anything, as we know Samantha would be. Anyone who knows Samantha knows.
	
	
		Samantha has not one but two love interests in this book. How did you shape her romantic personality, given that until now the only stories we have about Samantha are of a little girl?	

	That was tough because they are known as little girls, and so you’re adding in an element and you don’t want it to be uncomfortable. It would never be spicy. But the folks at American Girl were excited to have her have a love interest or two, but we were very careful about the historical accuracy of what that would mean as a couple. You wouldn’t hold hands in public. You would not kiss in public, and I had to fight hard to get that kiss [at the end of the book]. But they understood. The historical accuracy was really high on their list and I just wanted her to be caught between two men who are very different and offer a different side of the world.
	
		We lose Grandmary early on in the book and it becomes very emotional when Samantha tells her grandmother she loves her for the first time in her life on her deathbed. How did you decide to have Grandmary’s death be one of the catalysts for Samantha’s arc and how emotional to get?	

	Grandmary is such a beloved character, but I felt like, at that point, she’s been around a long time and this is what happens in a family: you have joy and then you have tragedy. And again, at the beginning of the book, Grandmary is such a strong connection for her and an anchor. To have that gone gives Samantha as a character freedom to explore different emotions and kind of figure out who she is and what she stands for because Grandmary’s voice is in her head throughout the entire book, which I love. I grew up in a very English family, my parents are both English and you would never say [‘I love you’] and so I brought that into that scene. What do you do so you don’t lose an opportunity that you’ll never have again?

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: How ‘American Girl’ Author Aged Up Samantha Parkington for Adult Historical Fiction Novel: ‘It Would Never Be Spicy’

title: Sophia Takal’s Psychosexual Thriller ‘Act One’ Acquired by Oscilloscope Laboratories (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Oscilloscope Laboratories has acquired U.S. rights to the psychosexual thriller “Act One” from writer-director Sophia Takal (“Always Shine,” “Black
body:
Oscilloscope Laboratories has acquired U.S. rights to the psychosexual thriller “Act One” from writer-director Sophia Takal (“Always Shine,” “Black Christmas”), and will release it in theaters in 2027.

	“Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” star Ella Beatty will play the leading role of Hannah, a sheltered seventeen-year-old aspiring actress. “Act One” follows Hannah as she joins an elite acting studio led by its magnetic founder, Melanie (Ari Graynor). Per the press release, “Drawn to Melanie’s intensity and increasingly extreme methods, Hannah throws herself into the work. But as dedication turns to obsession and the lines between performance, desire and manipulation blur, she is pulled into a dangerous game that tests how far she’ll go to become the artist she wants to be.”
	

	The film also stars Sinclair Daniel (“Insidious: The Red Door”), Tavi Gevinson (“Gossip Girl”), Elizabeth Reaser (“Twilight”) and Robert Sean Leonard (“House”).


	“I’m thrilled Oscilloscope is releasing ‘Act One,’” Takal said. “Getting to work with them again after ‘Always Shine’ feels like a homecoming. It’s heartening to know there are people out there with the taste, nerve and good sense to champion movies like ours. I can’t wait for audiences to see the incredible work of all the talented people who made this film!”

	The film debuted at Tribeca Festival on June 10. “Act One” is produced by Takal, Allison Rose Carter (Savage Rose Films), Julie Christeas (Tandem Pictures), Jon Read (Savage Rose Films), Stephanie Roush (Foxglove Films), and Julie Waters (Watermark Media). Executive producers are Evan Dyal of Watermark Media, Ryan Kampe of Visit Films, Lawrence Michael Levine, Allison and Jon Stockel and Marilyn White.

schema.headline: Sophia Takal’s Psychosexual Thriller ‘Act One’ Acquired by Oscilloscope Laboratories (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Skoop Media Launches New Crime Label Dutch Noir: ‘Range, Scale and Attitude’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Dutch international distributor Skoop Media has launched a new crime label Dutch Noir.

	Bowing at Mipcom, it’s a new international label for premiu
body:
Dutch international distributor Skoop Media has launched a new crime label Dutch Noir.

	Bowing at Mipcom, it’s a new international label for premium Dutch crime content spanning organized-crime drama, psychological thrillers, urban crime and heist series.

	The label kicks off with 17 titles from six producers, including four new Videoland Original series.


	“As one of Europe’s largest local streaming platforms, Videoland has the freedom to take risks and approach crime drama differently,” said Steven van Roosmalen, Head of Scripted.
	

	“We tell raw, direct stories that are deeply rooted in Dutch society, but explore universal themes. That’s exactly what makes Dutch crime so appealing to the audience.”

	At its core is the “Mocro Maffia” world, one of the most widely sold Dutch series of recent years. Over six seasons and several spin-offs, it has grown into a full crime universe, licensed to German and French-speaking Europe, Eastern Europe, Scandinavia, Belgium, Latin America and Japan.

	“Buyers are looking for the next ‘Mocro Maffia’. Dutch Noir is where they’ll find it,” said Pim van Collem, CEO of Snoop Media.

	“This slate has range, scale and attitude. It’s rooted in the reality of the drug trade in the Netherlands.”

	The Dutch Noir slate for Mipcom is led by Videoland Original “Narcostad,” created by “Mocro Maffia” lead actor Nasrdin Dchar. 

	The series follows teenagers recruited into Rotterdam’s drug economy, and will be presented alongside three further Videoland Originals: the second season of “Mocro Maffia” spin-off “Tonnano,” the fourth and final season of “Sleepers” and the short-form heist thriller “Rippers.”
	

	All four series are produced by Amsterdam-based Fiction Valley.

	Skoop Media doesn’t believe in “crime fatigue” – just the opposite.

	“Audiences aren’t tired of crime. They are always searching for new crime series, intrigued by bold raw characters, realistic and gritty storytelling. The international fanbase and proven sales of six Seasons of ‘Mocro Maffia’ in Europe, Latam and Asia is a proof that Dutch Noir stories travel,” added van Collem.

	The label will exemplify the best of Dutch crime series.

	“It’s rooted in a small country that isn’t just a backdrop for crime stories. It’s where most of Europe’s underworld is rooted.”

schema.headline: Skoop Media Launches New Crime Label Dutch Noir: ‘Range, Scale and Attitude’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Moana’ Live-Action Remake Sets Disney+ Streaming Release Date
description:
Moana of Motunui is coming to Disney+ soon. The live-action “Moana” remake will begin streaming on Disney+ on Oct. 21.

	Catherine Laga’aia makes he
body:
Moana of Motunui is coming to Disney+ soon. The live-action “Moana” remake will begin streaming on Disney+ on Oct. 21.

	Catherine Laga’aia makes her film debut as Moana in Disney’s latest live-action remake. The film follows her voyage to restore the heart of Te Fiti and help her village. Dwayne Johnson returns as the larger-than-life demigod Maui, joining Moana on her sea-faring adventure.


	The live-action “Moana” also stars Rena Owen as Gramma Tala, John Tui as Chief Tui, Frankie Adams as Sina and Jemaine Clement as Tamatoa the shiny king crab. Moana’s trusty pet pig Pua, confused rooster Heihei, the Kakamora and fiery Te Kā also return in the film.
	

	“’Moana‘ is a Disney live-action remake that escapes the Disney live-action remake blues — in fact, it soars above them,” Variety’s film critic Owen Gleiberman wrote in his review. “It’s the best of these movies I’ve seen…And it’s a rather odd bar, since this is an entire genre in which the definition of the genre is that it’s completely and totally unnecessary. These movies add nothing (except to Disney’s revenues).”

	“But in the case of ‘Moana,'” he continued, “for maybe the first time, if you told me that a child who’d never seen the animated version was going to see the remake, I’d say, ‘All good.’ Because the new ‘Moana’ truly delivers ‘Moana’: the beauty, the comic personality, the fairy-tale enchantment.”

	The film is directed by Thomas Kail, with a screenplay by Jared Bush and Dana Ledooux Miller. It features music by Mark Mancina and Lin-Manuel Miranda.
	

	Stream “Moana” on Disney+ starting Oct. 21.

schema.headline: ‘Moana’ Live-Action Remake Sets Disney+ Streaming Release Date

title: HBO Gives Two-Season Order to Animated Comedy ‘Merrick & Treves’ From ‘Archer’ Alums
description: HBO has given a two-season order to the new half-hour animated comedy “Merrick & Treves,” which comes from three alums from FX’s long-running “Arche
body:
HBO has given a two-season order to the new half-hour animated comedy “Merrick & Treves,” which comes from three alums from FX’s long-running “Archer”: Adam Reed, Casey Willis and Lucky Yates.

	Here’s the logline: “Set inside Queen Victoria’s top-secret Royal Temporal Constabulary, ‘Merrick & Treves’ follows a team of unlikely heroes as they voyage back and forth through time in an effort to stop Jack the Ripper.”
	

	Reed was the creator/exec producer of “Archer,” while Willis was also an exec producer while Yates was one of the show’s principal voice-over actors, playing Dr. Algernop Krieger and others. The trio also worked together on Adult Swim’s “Frisky Dingo.” 


	For “Merrick & Treves,” Reed, Willis and Yates will serve as co-creators and executive producers.

	“Adam, Casey and Lucky are exceptional comedic talents whom we have admired for years,” said HBO programming exec VP Amy Gravitt, who is the head of HBO & HBO Max comedy series. “We couldn’t be more excited to team up with them to bring the wholly original ‘Merrick & Treves’ to HBO audiences.”

	Also on the show, TFC Productions’ Joel Begleiter will executive-produce with Kelly Wu serving as co-executive producer.

	“The three of us are beyond excited to have found a home for ‘Merrick & Treves’ at HBO,” Reed, Willis and Yates said in a joint statement. “We can’t wait to start working with the creative team behind so many of our favorite shows. It’s actually quite daunting, now that we think about it. Like, holy shit, y’all. HBO.”
	

	If the names “Merrick & Treves” sound familiar, it’s because you may remember “The Elephant Man”:  Joseph Merrick is the name of the deformed individual who became famous after being exhibited in the late 1800s, while Frederick Treves was the young doctor who cared for him at London Hospital.

	“Archer” ran for 14 seasons and 145 episodes between 2009 and 2023 on FX/FXX. The series won four Primetime Emmys, including outstanding animated program. Reed is also known for “Chozen,” “Sealab 2021,” “12 oz. Mouse” and acting in “Robot Chicken.” Willis is known for voice roles on “Frisky Dingo,” “Sealab 2021″ and more before turning to producing.  Yates’ other credits include “Exploding Kittens,” “Cake” and “Hidden America With Jonah Ray.”

	Reed is repped by UTA, TFC Management and Yorn Levine.

schema.headline: HBO Gives Two-Season Order to Animated Comedy ‘Merrick & Treves’ From ‘Archer’ Alums

title: ‘SNL’ Sets Druski as First Online Content Creator to Host
description: Comedian and internet personality Druski will host the Nov. 7 episode of “Saturday Night Live.” Druski, aka Drew Desbordes, will be the first online
body:
Comedian and internet personality Druski will host the Nov. 7 episode of “Saturday Night Live.” Druski, aka Drew Desbordes, will be the first online creator to host the sketch show.

	Variety confirmed the news with multiple sources, though reps for “SNL” did not immediately respond to a request for comment and a rep for Druski declined to comment. 

	Druski joins a lineup of Season 52 hosts that has so far included Jalen Brunson, Dakota Johnson and Shane Gillis. “Obsession” breakout Indie Navarette is set to host the show’s Halloween episode with musical guest Gracie Abrams. Musical guests so far have have included Katseye, Turnstile and Rosaliá.
	

	So far, there have already been a number of viral moments to come out of “SNL” Season 52; Gillis not only dropped an accidental f-bomb during a Dr. Seuss sketch, but also sparked outrage over his misogynistic opening monologue. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” he said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it.” Dan Levy shared a video to Instagram following the episode, saying that he was “speechless that something like that can exist on live national television.”


	During the Oct. 3 episode, Taylor Swift surprised audiences by crashing Johnson’s monologue and stepping in as her breakup therapist.

	In Sept., “SNL” completed the Season 52 ensemble with two new cast members: Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie. Reiter is a stand-up comedian and actor who amassed a large following on TikTok and YouTube before she went on to star in Tim Robinson’s HBO comedy series “The Chair Company.” Belo-Osagie is a Brooklyn-based Nigerian American filmmaker and comedian. She is the creator of the event series Afrobeats Futura and the solo show “Saidah Gets Closure.”
	

	Excluding Chloe Fineman, Bowen Yang and Martin Herlihy, all members of the Season 51 cast returned for Season 52, the premiere episode of which aired on Sept. 26.

schema.headline: ‘SNL’ Sets Druski as First Online Content Creator to Host

title: Hillary Clinton to Co-Host Podcast on 2026 Midterm Elections With Kara Swisher for Vox Media, Owned by James Murdoch
description: Hillary Clinton will get behind the podcasting mic in “High Stakes,” where the former Secretary of State will weigh in on the 2026 U.S. midterm elec
body:
Hillary Clinton will get behind the podcasting mic in “High Stakes,” where the former Secretary of State will weigh in on the 2026 U.S. midterm elections in a new limited series with journalist Kara Swisher.

	Under the deal with Vox Media, Clinton will get a split of ad revenue generated from the episodes alongside Swisher.

	Vox Media is owned by James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems, which earlier this year bought the company’s podcast network, plus Vox.com and New York Magazine, reportedly for more than $300 million. Vox Media said “future collaborations” with Clinton and Swisher “are to come,” but didn’t elaborate.
	

	The Clinton-Swisher co-hosted special “High Stakes” premieres Wednesday, Oct. 14, and will run as a third episode of Swisher’s podcast for New York Magazine, “On With Kara Swisher,” weekly on Wednesdays. The series launches as control of the U.S. Congress hangs in the balance with the 2026 elections.


	“I don’t think the stakes for our country and the world have ever been higher than they are in November,” Clinton said in a statement provided by Vox Media. “People are hungry for real conversation about what’s happening in our democracy and what it will mean for their families, and I can’t think of a better partner for that than Kara. There will be some discussion, some debate and hopefully a lot of laughter.”

	Vox Media said that in the limited series, Swisher will be “drawing out the wickedly funny and sharp woman Americans may not have gotten to see before.” Clinton previously served as a guest host of “Pivot,” filling in for Swisher’s regular co-host Scott Galloway.
	

	“Think of this series [with Hillary Clinton] as ‘Pivot,’ but with an actual expert as my co-host,” Swisher joked. Clinton is “a global icon, she doesn’t hold back, and she’s going to bring the audience an invaluable perspective.”

	Jim Bankoff, Vox Media co-founder and CEO, commented, “I’m immensely proud to bring Secretary Clinton — a hero to millions who has had a profound impact making the world a better place — to Vox Media as she embarks on this next chapter of her media career.”

	Hillary Rodham Clinton spent her career in public service as an advocate, attorney, First Lady alongside President Bill Clinton, U.S. Senator, Secretary of State and presidential candidate. As First Lady, she traveled to more than 80 countries, standing up for human rights, democracy and civil society, according to her official bio. As a U.S. senator from New York, the first woman elected to statewide office in New York, she worked to expand economic opportunity and access to affordable health care. In her four years serving as President Barack Obama’s Secretary of State, she played a “central role” strengthening America’s global leadership, per her bio.

	In 2016, Clinton was the first woman nominated for president by a major U.S. political party. She won the national popular vote, with nearly 66 million votes, but lost the electoral college vote to Donald Trump. She is the author of 11 best-selling books, including “It Takes A Village” (1996) and the memoirs “Living History” (2003), “Hard Choices” (2014) and “What Happened” (2017).

	Separately from Murdoch’s deal to acquire Vox Media assets, PMC (parent of Variety) bought other Vox Media digital brands, including Eater, The Verge, SB Nation, Popsugar, The Dodo, Punch and Thrillist.

To perform his job, he sheds his clothes and personal effects to engage in an array of sexual acts, including vaginal and oral copulation, That is his professional pursuit, selling his body for cash to assist his curated clientele to achieve whatever sexual desire, fantasy or fetish is demanded."

Diddy said if Clayton was displeased with his menu offerings, or those requested off the menu, then he alone was empowered to change it or just say no ... but notes he did neither.

                          He Screwed Me Out Of 'Jack Reacher' Gig Due To Sofía

                                                                      |

                                  October 13, 2026

            Joe Manganiello's new memoir must be making some waves with Tom Cruise ... because the book speculates that the legendary actor screwed Joe out of a starring role ... and Joe thinks it's because he shares an ex with Tom -- Sofía Vergara!
      
    
            The New York Post got its hands on an advance copy of Joe's new book, "Bloodlines," and, in it, Joe claims that his team believes Tom prevented him from landing the lead role in Amazon's "Jack Reacher" series because the two men once dated Sofía.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In his memoir, Joe writes that Amazon bosses and production heads were initially dead set on giving the role to him ... but then the part suddenly went to another actor.
      

            Joe writes that his team speculated that Tom -- who played Reacher in two film versions of the book in 2012 and 2016 -- was behind the snub.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Here's how it all allegedly went down ... Joe writes that he met with one of the film's producers, Skydances' Don Granger, for an hour and a half. During their discussion, they allegedly talked about the backlash over Tom's small 5-foot-7 frame while the Reacher character in the book stands at an imposing 6-foot-5.
      
    
            Granger told Joe, "You are the closest thing to Jack Reacher that I've ever met in my entire life . . . You look like Reacher is described in the books . . . You have his effortless intelligence."
      
    
            In addition, Joe writes that Skydance owner David Ellison and Reacher book author Lee Child were "thrilled with my performance." 
      
    
            But everything went downhill after Amazon boss Jen Salke got upset about being cut out of the casting process by "primarily male producers," according to Joe.
      
    
            After Joe was given the bad news that he didn't get the part, his team suggested Tom, an executive producer on the TV show, might have put the kibosh on Joe and "vetoed my being cast on account of Sofía."
      
    
            Tom reportedly dated Sofía in 2005 ... years before her marriage to Joe.

            The Glendale Fire Department tells TMZ ... crews worked on him and, after some time, pronounced him dead on scene.
      
    
            Lucian had recently raised concern among fans after posting a series of alarming videos to Instagram. The clips appeared to show him spending much of his time on the street, prompting worried followers to question whether he was safe and doing okay.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told Lucian was taken into custody by Glendale PD on Saturday for being under the influence of controlled substance and again on Sunday for assault on an officer or emergency personal ... he was given a citation for both incidents and had a court date set on the day he died.
      
    
            Lucian was a judge, producer, and songwriter who worked on multiple seasons of RuPaul's show ... earning recognition for his contributions to the show's music and performances.
      
    
            He was 46.
